title: Chapter 219 – Everything You Want
html:
[Terrace Five – Jian]

The shadow of the Tenth does not walk into the Orchard. It is simply there, between one tick of the trees and the next, a tall hooded figure standing in the open gate with its hands folded in its sleeves, as though it had been waiting politely for someone to notice.

Jian is on his feet before he knows he has moved. The seed in his palm gives a hard bright beat. Beside him Yue has risen in one smooth motion, her right hand on a sword she has not drawn, her stone hand loose at her side. Pebble has stepped half in front of her. Hua is rigid, the mark in her palm blazing through the cloth of her sleeve like a coal.

Veyra Thann is the only one who does not stir.

Orrin, she says.

"Veyra." The voice that answers is soft and dry and kindly, with a rasp in it like a pen across parchment. It is not the voice he heard in the dream. It is the voice he has been hearing in the back of his mind since the Wall, at the edge of sleep: patient, courteous, utterly without heat. "You woke."

You woke me.

"I did." The hood tilts. "I am so glad. I was afraid you would not come."

I did not come.

"No." A gentle laugh. "You went the other way. It was the most natural thing in the world. I should have known you would. You never were one to walk into a room because you were asked."

Jian studies the figure.

He has seen it before, at Terrace Two, wearing the real mark and probing the ward on the Great Bell. Then it had been a shape, a patch of shade in the shape of a man. Now it has more. It has hands, the left one bandaged in gray cloth, the right bare, with a ring of ember light on the back that turns slowly, like a wheel. It has a face, or the beginning of one, a pale smooth oval under the hood with no features but the suggestion of a mouth. And it has weight. The grass does not bend beneath it, but the light does.

He lets the Scan open. It is a small, deliberate act, and it costs him an hour. He feels it go: a thin cold bead sliding out of the back of his skull, like a drop of water leaving a tap.

```
ARK-7 // SCAN (Soul band) [-1 hour]
Target: SHADOW OF THE TENTH
Type: PROJECTION. Not a person. Not a ghost.
Source: a mark-bearing hand at the Tenth Door, being used as a lens.
Hour: NONE. This target has no life to read.
Tether: one thread, running up through the Fifth Terrace's roof
toward Terrace Nine. Thickness: that of a hair.
Intent: PERSUASION. Confidence 94%.
Warning: every statement made by this target will be
true. Treat truth as a vector, not an assurance.
```

He closes the panel.

It has no hour, he thinks, toward Hua, toward the mark.

I know, she answers. I can feel the thread.

---

"I will not keep you," says the shadow. "I came only to offer a courtesy. You have come a long way, and you are tired, and I am in a position to make things a little easier."

We want nothing from you, says Veyra.

"You may feel differently when you hear it."

I will not.

"Then there is no harm in my saying it." The hooded head turns, slowly, taking in the circle of figures on the grass. "I am told you are a practical people. Let me be practical. The Road is long. The Terraces above this one run faster, and each hour you spend in them is worth more of the world's. A man who climbs from here to the Ninth will find that everyone he loved is dust. It need not be so."

"Why not?" says Yue.

She has not moved. Her voice is flat and cold.

"Because the Door can be opened from above," says the shadow. "I hold the key. I can open it. I can open it now, from here, to the Fifth Terrace, and you may walk through it into the top of the Seam, and be there in the time it takes to cross this grass. No fare. No stairs. No years."

The Bridge, thinks Hua.

"Not the Bridge. Something better." The smile is audible. "The Bridge costs the second key a day per Terrace. This costs nothing. It is a free gift, freely given. It is the one kindness the Door has left."

Nothing, thinks Jian.

Yes, says Veyra, very quietly. I know.

"You see," says the shadow, "I do not ask anything. I ask only that you let me help."

---

Jian watches it work.

It is a thing he has seen before, on the Silent Terrace, from the other side. A voice that offers. A hand held out. And the quiet, appalling pleasure of knowing that every word is true.

The shadow turns to Yue first.

"Madam Zhao," it says. "I am sorry about your hand."

Yue says nothing.

"It is a harsh price, for a small matter. Warmth. A cup of tea. The feel of a child's cheek." The voice is infinitely gentle. "I can give it back. I have the means. It is a trifle. A matter of moving one hour from one place to another." A pause. "You need only say yes."

Yue's face is white. Her stone hand has closed, slowly, into a fist.

"What is the price?"

"There is none."

"There is always a price."

"Not this time." The hood tilts. "You will have noticed that I have said nothing false. I have no reason to. I am what I am. I am a courtesy from a man who is very tired and wishes you well."

Her jaw works. Jian sees the muscle jump in her cheek. He sees, with a sick cold lurch of the stomach, exactly what she is holding at bay: a left hand that can feel a cup, a spring, the warmth of a hand in the dark. He sees thirty-one years of a sword. He sees a woman who chose the blade over the warmth, in a courtyard, in a dream.

Yue, he thinks.

She does not look at him.

"No," she says.

It comes out as a whisper. She tries again.

"No."

"Are you sure?"

"I made a choice." She lifts her chin. "I made it with my eyes open. If you give it back, it was never a choice. It was a loan." Her breath shudders. "I won't be loaned to."

The shadow is silent.

Then it turns, with a rustle of cloth, to Pebble.

---

"Pebble," it says.

The boy does not flinch. He is standing with his feet planted and his hands at his sides, and his shaved head gleams in the failing light. But his jaw has gone tight.

"You had a sister."

"Don't."

"Her name was Sun. She said no, when the Roll was read. She is sleeping in the Hall, in the fourth gallery, in the stack behind the bronze lamp." The voice is a velvet whisper. "I could wake her. Not all of the way. A little. Enough for her to open her eyes and say your name."

"That's not—"

"It would cost you nothing."

"She said no." Pebble's voice breaks. "She said she'd rather sleep."

"She said it in a moment of fear. You know that. You were there." The hooded head tilts. "A person who has been given a gift without being asked can always return it. That is the beauty of a gift. But she cannot return it if she is not awake."

Pebble makes a sound.

It is a small raw ugly noise, torn from somewhere below the ribs. His hands have come up, and he is gripping his own shoulders, and his eyes are enormous and wet.

Pebble, thinks Jian, urgently. Pebble, listen to me.

"I want to," says the boy.

I know.

"I want it so much."

I know. So did Mo Yan.

The name goes through him like a blade. Pebble's breath stops. His eyes go to Jian, wide, wet, uncomprehending, and Jian says, aloud, in the even voice he uses for bad news: "A little girl on the Silent Terrace was offered her mother's name for nothing. She wanted it more than anything. The Cartographer made a noise so that she would not take it."

"Who is the Cartographer?"

"A man who is stone, now." He holds the boy's gaze. "He is stone because the gift was free. And the thing that offers it is standing in that gate."

Pebble's lips are trembling.

"If I say no," he says, "will she wake?"

"If you say no, she will wake when you wake her."

"How?"

"By going up the Road, and coming down, and finding her bed in the fourth gallery, behind the bronze lamp." Jian breathes. "By earning it. By paying for it. By doing the thing you came here to do."

The boy is silent for a long time.

"No," he says.

It is very small. It is a whisper.

"No," he says again, louder. "Thank you. No."

And the shadow of the Tenth, standing in the gate, lets out a long soft sigh, like a man laying down a heavy burden.

---

The shadow turns, last of all, to Hua.

It takes its time. It lets the silence stretch, and the tick of the trees, and the long gold light slide across the grass. Hua has not moved. She is standing with her mark-hand pressed flat to her chest, and her small narrow face is bone white, and her eyes are fixed on the featureless oval under the hood with a kind of terrible attention.

"Warden," it says.

I know what you are, Hua thinks. You do not need to say it.

"I do not intend to say anything unkind." The voice is almost tender. "I only want to give you a small thing. A week. You lost a week, did you not? A week of memory, in the Hall of Ten Thousand Names, when the Warden's page was read. It was the week you spent with a girl of nine."

Hua's breath catches.

"You remember the shape of it," the shadow says. "The edges. A child in a cart-house, with a cloth over her mouth. A song, in the dark. You remember that you loved her. You do not remember why."

Stop.

"I can give it back. All of it. Every hour." The hood tilts. "It is not a large thing. It is a week. It is yours. I am only returning what was taken."

Stop it.

"Why would you refuse?" the voice murmurs, wondering. "It is not a trap. It is not a bargain. It is the gentlest gift in the world."

Hua's lips are trembling.

Jian watches her. He sees her hand go, slowly, to the burning mark in her palm. He sees her close her fingers over it, and he knows what she is doing, because he has watched her do it a dozen times in the last weeks: she is opening the channel. She is paying a day of her life to speak to the thing in the gate, because she will not do it aloud.

A week of memory, thinks Hua. The thought comes to him through the mark, faint and fierce, a note struck on a very small bell. I lost it. I gave it. Mo Yan wasn't a child I loved because it was easy. She was a child I loved because it cost me.

"It need cost you nothing—"

That is the point, says Hua. You do not understand it. You never will. A thing that costs me nothing is a thing I did not choose. A breath. I will remember her the hard way. I will remember her in pieces, in the dark, with the edges missing. And every piece I find will be mine.

The shadow is silent.

Take your gift, thinks Hua, and go.

The mark flares gold, once, and gutters. She sways. Jian steps forward and puts a hand under her elbow, and she leans on it, hard, with her eyes closed and her breath coming in short sharp gasps.

"A day," she whispers.

"I know."

"It's all right. It's only a day."

"I know," says Jian, again, and does not let go.

"Well," it says. "That is that."

Jian stiffens.

"I did hope you would take it." The voice has not changed. It is still gentle, still dry, still kind. But something under it has shifted, a hair's breadth, like a floorboard settling. "It is a great deal easier on all of us. But you are a stubborn people, and I have never held it against you." It turns its smooth, featureless face toward the old woman who has not moved from her stool. "Sorrel. I will ask you."

"No," says the Keeper of the Orchard.

"I have not said what it is."

"You are going to ask me to open the roof." Sorrel's voice is the dry rustle of wind in straw. "You are going to ask me to let the hours go up. All of them. The whole crop, all at once, to feed the Door." She sets her basket down. "And you are going to tell me that no one need be harmed, that the trees will be unburdened, that the passengers will be at peace. And all of it will be true."

"It will."

"And there will be a price."

"There will be no price."

"There is always a price, dear." She rises, creaking, and the green fire in her eyes is steady. "The price is that I stopped being the Keeper of the Fifth Terrace and became a lamp. I have been a lamp before. I did not like it."

The shadow does not move.

"I will not ask twice," it says.

"I know."

"The Door has need of the hours. It will take them. It would be a great deal kinder if you gave them."

"Kinder," says Sorrel, "for whom?"

And the shadow of the Tenth lifts its bare hand, and the ring of ember on the back of it flares white.

---

It happens very fast.

Jian sees the thread first: the thin bright thread of the tether, running from the shadow's palm up through the Orchard's roof. It thickens. It pulses. A shudder runs through the grass, and the trees on either side of the Row bend as in a gale, and every amber fruit on every bough lights from within, a thousand thousand tiny suns.

It's taking them, thinks Hua. Jian, it's taking the hours.

Stop it!

He does not know who he is speaking to. He lunges, and Yue lunges with him, her stone hand outstretched, her blade half-drawn. But the shadow does not turn. It simply opens its hand, and a wall of pale heat hits them like a fist, and Jian is thrown backward through the air with the breath driven from his body.

He lands on his side in the grass.

The Orchard is burning.

Not with fire. With light: a white, silent, terrible light that rises from every fruit on every tree in a single great column. It goes up through the brass leaves, up through the golden sky, up into the roof of the Terrace where the tether waits. He sees the tiny figures in the amber, thousands upon thousands, lifting their hands. He sees a man in a gray robe walking up a white stair. He sees a woman with a streak of white in her hair. He sees a nine-year-old girl with a black glass bell.

And in front of the column, small and stooped and unmoving, an old woman in a robe the color of dead grass stands with her arms spread wide.

Sorrel! cries Veyra.

"Go," says the Keeper.

She does not turn. Her voice is quite calm. In the white light, she looks like a thing carved of wood, a figure with a knotted face and bark for skin, and her green eyes burn like leaves in the sun.

"There is a stair at the far end of the Row. It goes to the Sixth. It has been waiting a long time." She takes a step forward, toward the column. "I will hold it. I have held it before."

You cannot hold it!

"Child," says Sorrel, with great tenderness, "I am the Orchard. I know my trees."

She puts her hands into the light.

---

Jian remembers the next few seconds as a series of images, disconnected, each of them lit from within.

He remembers Yue's hand on his collar, hauling him up. He remembers Pebble, weeping, with Hua's arm across his shoulders, running. He remembers the grass underfoot, long and gold and soundless, and the trees on either side going past in a blur of brass, each one lit from root to crown. He remembers the sound: a high thin note that begins at the edge of hearing and climbs and climbs, a single string pulled to breaking.

He remembers turning, once, at the far end of the Row.

The old woman stands in the middle of the white column with her arms thrown out. Her robe is burning. Her face is burning. The green fire in her eyes has spread across her whole body, running along her arms like vines, and the shadow of the Tenth stands before her with its hand outstretched, quite still, watching.

She is smiling.

Go, she says, in a voice that is not a voice but a rustle in the leaves. Climb. I have kept you long enough.

"Sorrel—"

Tell Orrin, she says, that I always did think he was a fool.

The column of light closes over her like a hand.

There is no sound. There is only a vast soft shock, a drop in pressure, as if the whole Terrace had inhaled. The trees go dark. One by one, down the long Row, the amber fruit gutters and fades, a thousand thousand tiny suns going out, until the Orchard of Hours is gray and cold and silent, and a single thread of white light goes up through its roof like a spider's line into the dark.

And Jian, who has been counting, who cannot help but count, feels the sum arrive in his mind with the terrible precision of a ledger closing:

Two hundred and four thousand hours. A lifetime for every fruit. The whole crop of the Fifth Terrace, fed in a single breath to the Door.

That is how it counts, he thinks. That is how it pays.

For a time no one moves.

Pebble has sunk to his knees at the foot of the stair, with both hands over his mouth. Hua is standing with her eyes shut and her lips moving, and Jian recognizes the oath of the Wardens, the old one, the one for the dead: I will keep the count. I will not close my eyes while there is a name unread. She says it twice. Then she opens her eyes and looks at her burning mark, and her face is wet.

"She knew," she says. "She knew it was coming. She said she'd been a lamp before."

"She was the Orchard," says Yue. Her voice is rough. "She was never anything else."

"She could have gone."

"No." Yue stares at the dark trees. "She couldn't. I watched her. She wasn't deciding. She was just standing where she'd always stood, and when the thing came, she was there." Her stone hand opens and closes at her side. "I know that kind of courage. It isn't brave. It's just the shape of a person who's done one job for four hundred years."

Nobody says anything.

Jian finds that he is shaking. Not the old tremor, which is gone, but something deeper, a cold tide moving up from the base of his spine. He thinks of the wrinkled walnut face, the leaf-dark eyes, the voice like wind in dry straw. I am so very bored, she had said. I have not had an audience in centuries. He thinks that he had liked her. He thinks that he had not said so.

The panel appears at the edge of his vision. He does not want to read it.

```
ARK-7 // LEDGER
Terrace Five: ORCHARD OF HOURS: STATUS: DEPLETED.
Hours consumed by the Door: 204,118.
Sitting: no longer possible on this Terrace.
Nascent Soul seed: Jian (stage 0), Yue (stage 0), Hua (stage 0),
Pebble (Core only). Seeds will not mature without a second
year's sitting. Next known source: Terrace Six.
Lifespan: 90y 212d (Scan, 2 readings). Next fare: 1 year.
Note: The Door has now burned the fares of every passenger
since the Founders. It will not need to ask again for a long time.
```

A long time, he thinks.

Or a short one, answers Veyra's voice, cool in his mind. That depends on what it means to do with them.

He looks at her.

She has not moved from the foot of the new stair. Her ruined hand is pressed against her breastbone, and her face, in the gray light, looks as if it had been carved from the same stone as the Keepers on the Fourth. But her eyes are open, and they are fixed on the dark Orchard behind them, on the place where a small stooped woman in a robe the color of dead grass once stood with her arms thrown wide.

She always did think he was a fool, says Veyra, softly. It was the only thing we ever agreed on.

Pebble has risen. He stands with his arms wrapped round himself, looking at the dark Row, at the husks of the trees, at the place where the grass is scorched in a perfect circle. He has stopped weeping. There is an odd, flat steadiness in his face, the look of a boy who has just been shown the size of the thing he is climbing toward.

"She said it was a lamp," he says. "That's what the Door does. It turns people into lamps."

"Yes," says Jian.

"Then I'd like to be the one who puts it out."

Yue turns her head and looks at him for a long moment. Then she nods, once, and says nothing at all, and picks up the water skin he has dropped, and hangs it on her own shoulder.

"Carry it later," she says. "Walk now."

"Jian," says Veyra Thann.

Her voice is very quiet. She is standing at the foot of a stair he has not seen before, a narrow white stair of unfamiliar stone, rising into a pale mist. Her hood is thrown back. Her face is gray and still and old.

It is time, she says. The Sixth is waiting. And I think, if we are quick, that we may still arrive before it notices we are gone.

He looks back.

The Orchard is dark. In the gate, small and tall and hooded, with its bare hand lowered, the shadow of the Tenth is watching them go. It does not follow. It does not speak. But as he turns toward the stair, the voice comes to him one last time, soft and dry and kind, from a great distance:

Everything you want, Lin Jian. I do so hope you will remember that I offered.

He takes the first step.

Behind him, in the cold gray silence of the Fifth Terrace, a single amber fruit, the last one, falls from its bough and rolls across the grass to his feet. It is whole. It is unburnt. And inside it, very small and very clear, a tiny figure in a gray robe and a plain cloak lifts her hand and waves.

He does not pick it up.

He climbs.
